planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Osprey tolerates a wide range of light but the ice-white flowers show best against the dark-green foliage in some shade. Divide congested clumps every 3-4 years in early spring.

directions: Plant divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Osprey is a widely grown Andersoniana Group spiderwort cultivar prized for its clear, ice-white, three-petaled flowers, each centered with a small tuft of violet-blue at the base of the petals and topped with bright yellow stamens, a striking contrast against the strappy, arching, blue-green foliage. Like all garden spiderworts, individual flowers open in the morning and collapse by afternoon, but the clump produces a long, heavy succession of buds from late spring through midsummer, with a lighter rebloom possible in fall if sheared back after the first flush. Osprey holds an RHS Award of Garden Merit and is valued for bringing a cool white note to shaded and partly shaded borders where flower color options are limited. Cut the whole clump back hard after flowering fades or when foliage looks tired in summer heat to encourage fresh growth and a second bloom cycle.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or fall in moist to average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Zwanenburg Blue is one of the deepest and most saturated blue-flowered spiderwort cultivars and shows its color best with some afternoon shade. Divide crowded clumps every 3-4 years in early spring to keep plants vigorous.

directions: Plant divisions in moist, average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Zwanenburg Blue is a Dutch-bred Andersoniana Group cultivar producing an especially deep, rich blue-violet flower color, each triangular, three-petaled bloom accented by sulphur-yellow stamens against arching, strap-shaped green foliage. As with all spiderworts, individual flowers last only a single day, opening at dawn and closing by afternoon, but the plant produces a long parade of buds over six to eight weeks from late spring into summer. Partial shade, especially afternoon shade, keeps the flower color from washing out in strong sun and helps the foliage stay fresher through summer heat. Cut plants back hard after the main bloom flush or whenever foliage becomes ragged to promote tidy new growth and a possible fall rebloom.
sources: Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder — Tradescantia (Andersoniana Group) 'Zwanenburg Blue'
Royal Horticultural Society — Tradescantia (Andersoniana Group) 'Zwanenburg Blue'

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or fall in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Karminglut's flower color is most vivid where it gets some relief from the hottest afternoon sun. Divide clumps every 3-4 years in early spring to maintain bloom vigor.

directions: Plant divisions in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Karminglut (German for 'carmine glow') is a German-bred Andersoniana Group cultivar grown for its shocking magenta-pink to rosy-red flowers, a distinctly warmer color than the blue and purple shades typical of most garden spiderworts. The three-petaled blooms, each lasting only a single morning, open in long succession over many weeks from late spring through summer against clumps of arching, blue-green, strap-like foliage. The saturated pink-red flower color makes Karminglut a useful companion for blue- and purple-flowered perennials, providing a warm contrast note in mixed borders and partly shaded woodland-edge plantings. Shear the clump back after the first flowering flush fades to tidy the foliage and encourage renewed bloom later in the season.
sources: Plant Delights Nursery — Tradescantia x andersoniana 'Karminglut'

common_name: Variegated Small Leaf Spiderwort (Striped Wandering Willie)

planting.note: Root 3-4 inch stem cuttings in water or moist potting mix; cuttings root readily in 1-2 weeks. In zone 9-11, establish in spring in shaded beds or containers; elsewhere grow as a houseplant or hanging basket subject year-round. Some direct morning sun keeps the white striping crisp, but foliage reverts toward plain green in deep shade.

directions: Root stem cuttings in water or moist mix and plant in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade with some gentle morning sun; Tradescantia fluminensis 'Variegata' (also sold as 'Albovittata') carries the same glossy, oval, fleshy leaves as plain small leaf spiderwort but boldly striped in white above with a purple-flushed underside, and stems that turn pinkish in brighter light. Small three-petaled white flowers appear intermittently when temperatures stay warm. CAUTION — like the green species, this cultivar spreads rapidly by rooting at every leaf node and is classified as invasive in Florida, New Zealand, and other warm-temperate regions, so confine it to containers or fully contained garden beds well away from natural areas. Watch for and remove any all-green reverted shoots promptly, since the plain form grows more vigorously than the variegated one and will gradually overtake it if left unchecked.
sources: Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder — Tradescantia fluminensis 'Variegata'
North Carolina State University Extension — Tradescantia fluminensis Plant Toolbox

common_name: Cobweb Spiderwort (White Velvet, White Gossamer Plant)

planting.note: Root 3-4 inch stem cuttings in slightly moist, fast-draining succulent mix; cuttings callus and root within 1-2 weeks. In zone 9-11 plant out in spring in bright, partly shaded beds or rock gardens; elsewhere grow year-round as a houseplant or summer container plant. Let the soil surface dry between waterings, since this species is more drought-tolerant than other tradescantias.

directions: Root stem cuttings in well-drained succulent mix and grow in bright, indirect light to partial shade; cobweb spiderwort is a Mexican succulent species instantly recognizable by its small, thick, overlapping gray-green leaves densely coated in fine white, cobweb-like hairs that give the whole plant a soft, felted, silvery appearance quite unlike the smooth or glossy leaves of most other tradescantias. Small pink to magenta three-petaled flowers appear at branch tips, mainly in fall and winter when day length shortens. Because its succulent leaves store water, cobweb spiderwort tolerates brighter light and drier soil than trailing species such as T. zebrina or T. fluminensis, and it resents constantly wet, humid conditions that cause the fuzzy leaves to rot or mat down. In zone 9-11 it makes a distinctive textural groundcover or rock garden accent; elsewhere it is an easy, low-maintenance houseplant that benefits from a rest period with reduced water over winter.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox — Tradescantia sillamontana
